study.title: Luke 15 The God Who seeks, receives and restores the lost
study.overview: Luke 15 brings together three parables linked by the same idea: something or someone is lost, is sought and, when found, provokes joy. The chapter responds to the criticism of the Pharisees and scribes against Jesus for welcoming publicans and sinners. The first two parables show that the loss of someone loved causes sadness, but the reunion generates a feast; the third deepens this by presenting a father who receives with compassion the repentant son and also confronts the hardness of the eldest son. The chapter teaches that God's grace is not the approval of sin, but the restoration of the lost, and that the right joy before the repentance of others is to participate in the joy of the Father.

outline.title: Jesus defends his welcome to sinners with two short parables
outline.explanation: The publicans and sinners approach to hear Jesus, while Pharisees and scribes murmur for receiving such people and eating with them. Jesus responds with the parables of the lost sheep and of the lost coin, in which the diligent search ends in joy when what was lost is found. The central point is that there is joy in heaven and before the angels of God when a sinner repents.

outline.title: The youngest son gets lost, repentant back and is greeted with restoration
outline.explanation: In the parable of the prodigal son, the request of the youngest son is offensive, as if the father was already dead to him. After wasting the goods and starving, he remembers the abundance of the father's house and decides to return, confessing his sin. The father sees him from afar, compassionate, embraces him and publicly restores him with clothes, ring, sandals and party, declaring that his son was dead and revived.

outline.title: The eldest son reveals the hardness of heart and the father calls him to joy
outline.explanation: The eldest son gets angry at the celebration and refuses to enter, accusing his father of injustice for never giving him a kid, while this son returned after wasting the goods. The father reminds him that he has always been with him and that all that is of his father is also his. The ending remains open, inviting the older brother and the religious listeners - to join the joy necessary for the restoration of the lost brother.

study.context: The chapter begins with the approach of publicans and sinners to hear Jesus, while Pharisees and scribes murmur against their practice of receiving and eating with them. The notes indicate that publicans were despised for working for the Roman authorities and, in many cases, for their corruption. The scenario shows the clash between Jesus" mercy and the self-sufficient posture of religious leaders.
study.theology: Luke 15 presents the saving initiative of God: he seeks the lost, receives the repentant, and rejoices in his restoration. The three parables show that repentance does not buy forgiveness; he is the return response to the Father who already moves in compassion. The figure of the father running to meet the child communicates abundant grace, not a cold or merely legal welcome. At the same time, the chapter confronts both the explicit rebellion of the younger son and the proud justice of the eldest. Thus, the text teaches that sinners are received by divine mercy, but also that disciples and leaders can get lost inside the house when they do not share the Father's heart. Restoration includes forgiveness, identity rehabilitation and festive communion; therefore, the right attitude to grace is to rejoice in what God does.

scholarViews.insight: The parable ends openly, for it does not say how the eldest son answered; this acts as an invitation for religious leaders to react to Jesus" call to the Kingdom.
The three parables have the same goal: to show how pleasing to God is the conversion of sinners and how he receives them with joy when they repent.

By saying that the brother was found, the father corrects the hostile language of the eldest son: the one who was previously dead in sin and lost was now brought back, and this should arouse tenderness instead of contempt.

questions: Which character do I identify with more in this parable: the youngest son, the eldest or the father?
Is my reaction to another person's repentance before God or resentment by comparison?
Is there any area in which I need to return to the Father with sincere confession, without negotiating my own dignity?
study.practice: Practice three concrete answers to the chapter: first, examine yourself honestly and turn to God with clear confession; secondly, welcome generously who demonstrates genuine repentance, without reminding him only of the past; third, ask God for a heart similar to that of the Father, able to rejoice in the restoration of people who once seemed distant. It is also useful to observe whether his religiosity has more of the child older than the Father: external closeness to God can coexist with lack of compassion.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided about Matthew Henry are partially truncated in some excerpts, so the synthesis was built only from the content effectively visible. It is not safe to state historical, geographical or archaeological details that do not appear in the biblical text or in the notes. The confessional interpretations presented here are possible evangelical readings of the chapter, not undeniable definitions of the text.
